q-126851.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247905/assets/e9892ef4efa3481ad02f7b8e38f1bae1876b196627204521d011656010297281.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=6,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=4,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
q-126851.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247905/assets/b20b2b911c2a417c26fa951d9b28efa296c265df25e9d06b635ef4846267b93b.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+6+4 \\  & =26.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ and $Q(x,y)=({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3}).$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,dx+({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}-(-4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\cdot \frac{3{r}^{5}}{5}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =(1-1)\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
